User plans to apply for a U.S. green card and will consult an immigration attorney about their application and their parents’ immigration status. Parents have reportedly stayed with them for nine months, helped substantially with paperwork, and the prior assistant assumed an overstay; this must be verified from visa category, admission/status, and authorized stay because there is no blanket six-month limit for B-2 visitors. Determine whether they are in authorized status, whether an extension/change of status was timely filed, and whether any unlawful-presence departure/entry bars apply.

Parents should disclose exact entries, visa/status, I-94s, extensions, and exits. A nine-month stay alone does not necessarily make someone inadmissible. Unlawful-presence accrual depends on status and dates, begins only after certain violations, and is generally counted when the person departs; a nine-month period may fall below the 180-day unlawful-presence threshold. Undocumented presence is not automatically a waiver ground.

If a relevant ground of inadmissibility applies, the applicable procedure may involve I-601, I-601A, or another form/process; ordinary overstay is not automatically waive
trajectory: User is considering applying for a U.S. green card and wants guidance on eligibility, documents, filing steps, timelines, financial requirements, and what happens after submitting a petition. Their parents have lived with them in the U.S. for six months, help with household chores and cooking, and are taking English classes; the family has a positive relationship. User is unsure whether nonworking parents’ finances and expenses must be included, especially if the parents are included in the immigration application. They have also asked about common application mistakes and the post-filing process.
